title: South Africa’s payments remain cash-heavy for volume while cards carry higher-value transactions across income groups
source_unit: South African Reserve Bank, Payments Study Report 2023, combining Survey of Consumer Payment Choice and Diary of Consumer Payment Choice
geography: South Africa; adults aged 18 years and older, with nationwide payment diaries, income-group, province, demographic, and payment-method dimensions

denominator.unit: Diary of Consumer Payment Choice panellists completing or contributing to the three-month diary programme; 210,207 recorded payments worth R111.2 million

cash_payment_volume_share.unit: percent of estimated payment volume recorded through cash

cash_payment_value_share.unit: percent of estimated payment value recorded through cash

cash_average_transaction.unit: South African rand average cash payment per transaction

debit_payment_volume_share.unit: percent of estimated payment volume recorded through debit cards

debit_payment_value_share.unit: percent of estimated payment value recorded through debit cards

debit_average_transaction.unit: South African rand average debit-card payment per transaction

mechanism.value: Cash and cards are not simple substitutes: cash dominates transaction count while debit cards carry much more transaction value, so payment modernization changes the value and visibility of consumption unevenly

observations.method: SARB payment diary estimates from the DCPC, which recorded actual payments over repeated three-day diary cycles; volume and value shares are estimated from weighted diary transactions.
observations.uncertainty: The diary captures payment instruments rather than total consumption, merchant acceptance, income effects, or consumer welfare; payment-method categories and weighting may not be directly comparable to administrative transaction totals.
observations.subgroup: South African adults aged 18 years and older, with cash and debit-card transaction comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cash can remain preferred for privacy, acceptance, budgeting, or low-value purchases, while card use for higher values may reflect merchant infrastructure or safety rather than preference alone.

denominator.unit: Diary of Consumer Payment Choice panellists contributing to the weighted three-month diary; income groups use personal gross monthly income

low_income_population_share.unit: percent of weighted diary population with personal gross monthly income below R5,000

low_income_payment_value_share.unit: percent of total payment value represented by the low-income group

low_income_average_payment.unit: South African rand average payment per transaction for the low-income group

high_income_population_share.unit: percent of weighted diary population with personal gross monthly income above R25,000

high_income_payment_value_share.unit: percent of total payment value represented by the high-income group

high_income_average_payment.unit: South African rand average payment per transaction for the high-income group

mechanism.value: Payment value is concentrated above population share: high-income consumers generate disproportionate payment value while lower-income consumers transact at much smaller average amounts, shaping who is visible to digital commerce and loyalty systems

observations.method: SARB weighted diary analysis using personal gross monthly income bands; payment volume means transaction count and payment value means transaction rand value.
observations.uncertainty: Income grouping is self-reported and the diary measures recorded payment flows, not wealth, unmet demand, total household consumption, or causal purchasing power.
observations.subgroup: South African adult diary panellists by personal gross monthly income group.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher payment values may reflect recurring bills, business transactions, household composition, or different merchant access rather than greater cultural or consumer wellbeing.

observations.period: 2023; stated payment use versus diary-recorded digital methods

denominator.unit: SARB Survey of Consumer Payment Choice (SCPC) recall sample versus Diary of Consumer Payment Choice (DCPC) weighted payment sample; denominators differ and are not interchangeable

digital_methods_recall_population_share.unit: percent of SCPC consumer population reporting use of the report’s digital-payment-method category

digital_methods_diary_population_share.unit: percent of DCPC consumer population represented by recorded digital-payment-method transactions in the three-month diary

cardless_recall_population_share.unit: percent of SCPC consumers reporting cardless-payment use

cardless_diary_population_share.unit: percent of DCPC consumer population represented by cardless-payment transactions

crypto_payment_recall_share.unit: percent of SCPC population reporting crypto assets as a payment method, mainly for investment

crypto_payment_diary_share.unit: percent of recorded DCPC transactions using crypto-asset payments

mechanism.value: Reported annual adoption and observed near-term transactions are different stages: intermittent, niche, or context-specific digital methods can appear widespread in recall but rarely in a short transaction diary

observations.method: Comparison of the SARB SCPC recall instrument, which asks about use in the past year, with the DCPC three-month payment diary; the report explicitly warns that the measures and category definitions differ.
observations.uncertainty: The apparent gap is not a prevalence estimate or causal contradiction: recall period, method definitions, intermittent use, sample composition, and diary compliance all differ.
observations.subgroup: South African adults in the SCPC and DCPC payment-study samples.
observations.counterinterpretation: A method can be important for occasional high-salience payments while absent from a short diary; low observed frequency does not imply low perceived usefulness or future growth.

related_sources.claim: SARB official publication page describing the first national Payments Study and linking its report and executive summary.
SARB payments-study dissemination page describing consumer payment instruments, cash persistence, cards, banking apps, and digital-payment limitations.

boundary: This record adds a South African payment-choice and transaction-diary layer to the cultural, social, and consumer atlas. It does not establish causal payment substitution, cultural spending, merchant behavior, financial welfare, or representativeness beyond the documented survey design.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: SARB 66-page Payments Study Report reviewed; SCPC/DCPC design, diary sample, 210,207 payments, cash/debit summary tables, income-group payment-value analysis, recall-versus-diary definitions, and method limitations checked.
